newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU sees faster growth in 97.
newsitem.headline: EU sees faster growth in 97.

text.p: Economic growth in the European Union is expected to advance at a rate of 1.6 percent in 1996, rising to 2.3 percent in 1997, the European Commission said Wednesday.

In its twice-yearly review of economic conditions in the 15-nation bloc, the EU's executive also said 12 countries are expected to bring their deficits down to no more than 3.0 percent of gross domestic product in 1997.
Countries wishing to join a single currency in 1999 must meet a series of economic tests in 1997, among which are relatively tight budget policies.
By the Commission's calculations, only Greece, Italy and Britain are seen not meeting the Maastricht treaty's deficit criteria.

On the economic front, the Commission's estimates for growth in the EU were little changed from its last forecast in the spring. At that time, the Commission saw GDP rising at a rate of 1.5 percent in 1996, followed by a 2.4 percent pickup next year.
For Germany, the EU's economic powerhouse, economic growth was revised sharply upward in 1996, from 0.5 percent to 1.4 percent.

EU monetary affairs commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy told at a news conference: "For the majority of member states the biggest part of budgetary consolidation has been put on the road in a credible manner."

While the better economic outlook in Germany contributed greatly to the upbeat assessment for next year, the Commission noted that a slackening in growth in Italy -- from 1.8 percent to 0.8 percent -- held back the overall gain.
"The slowdown in Italy is linked to the appreciation of the lira and to the process of domestic stabilisation," the Commission's report said.
Without the dampening effect of Italy's slower growth, EU GDP growth would be a quarter of percentage point higher in 1996 and 1997.
